lead: A triple integral adds up a function of three variables over a solid in space, and it is computed as three nested ordinary integrals. It exists because many quantities — mass of a block, charge inside a battery, heat in a room — pile up over thickness as well as over length and width. Limits are read from the inequalities that describe the solid, one variable at a time, from the innermost of Chapter 5.1 outward. Engineers use it for volume, centre of mass and flow totals.
prereq: You need: double integrals as iterated integrals and Fubini's theorem from Chapter 5.1, and the region-reading habits from Chapter 5.2.

sections.h3: From a box to a solid

blocks.text: A box B is the set of points (x, y, z) with a ≤ x ≤ b, c ≤ y ≤ d and p ≤ z ≤ q. All six limits are constants. The triple integral of f over B is written ∭<sub>B</sub> f(x, y, z) dV, where dV is a small volume element and f is the density-like quantity being added up.

Fubini's theorem for three variables says the order does not matter for a box. You may integrate x first, then y, then z, or any of the six orders, and get the same number. For a box this is written with all limits constant:
∭<sub>B</sub> f dV = ∫<sub>p</sub><sup>q</sup> ∫<sub>c</sub><sup>d</sup> ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x, y, z) dx dy dz
blocks.where: a, b are the x limits; c, d the y limits; p, q the z limits; f is the integrand; dx, dy, dz are the three ordinary integrations, done from inner to outer.

blocks.text: To evaluate, work from the inside out. The inner integral treats y and z as constants and produces a function of y and z. The middle integral kills y. The outer integral leaves a plain number.

For a solid that is not a box — a slab, a cylinder or a pyramid, for example — the outer limits stay constant but the inner ones become functions of the variables outside them. Suppose a solid S sits above a region R in the xy-plane and between the surfaces z = g₁(x, y) and z = g₂(x, y). Then dV = dz dy dx with z running from g₁ to g₂.
∭<sub>S</sub> f dV = ∬<sub>R</sub> [ ∫<sub>g₁(x,y)</sub><sup>g₂(x,y)</sup> f(x, y, z) dz ] dA
blocks.where: R is the shadow of the solid on the xy-plane; g₁ and g₂ are the lower and upper surfaces; dA is the area element dx dy; the inner integral is done first for fixed (x, y).

blocks.text: Reading limits is the whole skill. Sketch the solid. Ask which variable has the simplest constant range — usually z from floor to roof. That variable goes outermost. Then project the shadow and read the double integral limits exactly as in Chapter 5.1.

sections.h3: Choosing an order and using volume

items: Write the inequalities that define the solid: for each variable, what is it between?
Pick the variable whose limits are plain constants; make it the outer integral.
For the next variable, fix the outer one and find its range inside the solid.
For the innermost variable, fix the other two and read its range as a function of them.
Integrate inside out, simplifying after each stage.
Check the answer's sign and rough size: integrating 1 over the solid must give its volume.
The integrand must not depend on the innermost variable after that integration is done.
A dependent limit may contain only variables that are still free at that stage.
If an inner integral looks impossible, try swapping the order — the same trick as Chapter 5.2, one dimension up.
Setting f = 1 gives the volume of the solid; that is the topic of Chapter 5.5.
Cylindrical and spherical versions with a Jacobian live in Chapter 5.3.

blocks.text: A common use in Indian engineering courses is mass from density. If a metal block has density ρ(x, y, z) kilograms per cubic metre, then the mass is ∭ ρ dV, and its units come out in kilograms because dV carries m³.

figure.caption: The unit cube is split into three ordinary integrals, all with constant limits from 0 to 1, and the three passes give 3/2 for the integrand x + y + z.

spec.title: Triple integral over the unit cube
spec.aria: A downward flow from the unit cube 0 to 1 in x, y, z, to the inner x integral, then the middle y integral, then the outer z integral, ending at the value 3/2.

examples.question: Evaluate ∭<sub>B</sub> (x + y + z) dV where B is the unit cube 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ 1.
steps: The solid is a box, so all six limits are constants and any order works. Take the order dx dy dz, with x innermost, y middle, z outer.
Inner integral in x, with y and z held constant: ∫₀¹ (x + y + z) dx = [x²/2 + xy + xz] from 0 to 1 = 1/2 + y + z.
Middle integral in y: ∫₀¹ (1/2 + y + z) dy = [y/2 + y²/2 + zy] from 0 to 1 = 1/2 + 1/2 + z = 1 + z.
Outer integral in z: ∫₀¹ (1 + z) dz = [z + z²/2] from 0 to 1 = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2.
Check by symmetry: each of the three single-variable pieces contributes ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2, and there are three of them, giving 3/2. The answer is positive, as x + y + z ≥ 0 on the cube.
examples.answer: The triple integral equals 3/2, a pure number with no units.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction

# after integrating x and y: 1 + z
# outer antiderivative: ∫ (1 + z) dz = z + z²/2
def outer_antiderivative(z):
    return z + z * z / 2

value = outer_antiderivative(Fraction(1)) - outer_antiderivative(Fraction(0))
print(value)
print(float(value))

traps: Using constant limits for a non-box solid. The outermost limits must be constants; inner limits may be constants or may depend only on variables outside them.
Putting a dependent limit on the wrong variable, for example writing z from 0 to x² when the solid is bounded by x = √z.
Forgetting that after the inner integration the variable is gone, so the next limit must not mention it.
Dropping the units: a density in kg/m³ times dV in m³ gives kg, but a bare integral of 1 gives a volume in m³, not a number.
Assuming order does not matter for a non-box solid. The value is the same, but the limits must be re-read for each new order.

quiz.q: State Fubini's theorem for a triple integral over a box.
quiz.a: For f continuous on the box a ≤ x ≤ b, c ≤ y ≤ d, p ≤ z ≤ q, the triple integral equals the three nested integrals ∫ₚ<sup>q</sup>∫<sub>c</sub><sup>d</sup>∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f dx dy dz, and the order of the three integrations may be changed freely.

quiz.q: Why does the innermost integral's limit sometimes contain other variables while the outermost limit does not?
quiz.a: Working from inside out, at the innermost stage y and z are fixed, so the range of x can depend on them. By the time we reach the outermost integral, all other variables have been integrated away, so its limits must be plain constants describing the full extent of the solid.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∭<sub>S</sub> z dV where S is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ x.
quiz.a: Inner in z: ∫₀ˣ z dz = x²/2. Middle in y, constant integrand: x²/2 times (1 − 0) = x²/2. Outer in x: ∫₀¹ x²/2 dx = 1/6. Final answer 1/6.

quiz.q: Find the volume of the solid 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ x + y by a triple integral of 1.
quiz.a: Inner in z: x + y. Middle in y: xy + y²/2 from 0 to 1 gives x + 1/2. Outer in x: x²/2 + x/2 from 0 to 2 gives 2 + 1 = 3. Volume = 3 cubic units.

quiz.q: A student writes ∭<sub>S</sub> f dV = ∫₀¹∫₀¹∫₀¹ f dx dy dz for the solid bounded by z = x² + y² and z = 1. What is wrong, and what is the correct inner limit?
quiz.a: The solid is not a box. In the student's order z is outermost, and z from 0 to 1 is the correct overall range. The error is the constant x and y limits from 0 to 1: at fixed z the cross-section is x²+y² ≤ z, not the unit square. Equivalently, change order and put z inner from x²+y² to 1 over the unit disc x²+y² ≤ 1: ∭ f dV = ∬<sub>disc</sub> ∫<sub>x²+y²</sub><sup>1</sup> f dz dA.

quiz.q: Without computing, argue that ∭<sub>B</sub> (x + y + z) dV over the unit cube is the same in all six orders of integration.
quiz.a: All six limits are constants, so the box is a product of intervals. Fubini's theorem applies to the continuous integrand x + y + z on that box and allows any order. Symmetry confirms it: the sum separates into three identical single integrals each equal to 1/2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Triple integrals become the volume integrals behind Gauss's divergence theorem in Unit 6, where a flux through a closed surface is traded for an integral over the enclosed solid. In engineering practice the same nesting appears in finite element software, which chops a part into small tetrahedra and sums a simple rule over each. In machine learning, Monte Carlo integration replaces the inner sums by random samples when the dimension climbs past four or five. Search for 'Gauss divergence theorem', 'Gaussian quadrature on tetrahedra' or 'Monte Carlo integration' to go further.
